name: Electrolysis
lead: Electrolysis, in appearance contexts, is a hair-removal method in which a practitioner inserts a fine sterile probe into each hair follicle and applies electrical current to destroy the follicle's growth centre. It is used for the face, brows, hairline and body, and is distinct from the chemistry process of the same name [1][2].

Wikipedia's hair-removal article describes electrolysis (electrology) as practised in the United States since 1875 and as the only method it identifies as recognised by the FDA for permanent hair removal [3]. Treatment is done one follicle at a time, so courses for larger areas commonly run for many months or longer [2].
infobox: Often 15 to 30 sessions over 12 to 18 months for small to medium areas [2]
About $50 to $150 per hour, higher in some cities [2]
Needle epilators proposed as Class II devices; about 31 states license electrologists [2]

paras: Grokipedia describes three approaches. Galvanic electrolysis uses direct current to generate sodium hydroxide in the follicle and is slower, at roughly 10 to 60 seconds per follicle. Thermolysis uses high-frequency current to heat the follicle, at roughly 1 to 5 seconds per follicle, and may have higher regrowth rates. Blend combines the two and takes longer per hair but is used for stubborn or curved hairs [2].

According to Grokipedia, St. Louis ophthalmologist Charles E. Michel introduced electrolysis in 1875 to treat ingrown eyelashes. Paul M. Kree patented a multiple-needle epilator in 1916, thermolysis was described in the 1920s, and a blend method followed, with sources giving conflicting dates in the 1930s and 1940s. Transistor machines in the 1970s and multi-probe systems in the 1980s later improved speed and precision [2].

Grokipedia cites a success rate of about 93 percent attributed to the American Academy of Dermatology and says some regrowth is seen in roughly 15 to 40 percent of cases, which it notes sits uneasily with the word permanent [2]. It also reports that hormonal conditions such as polycystic ovary syndrome can require more sessions, and that laser and IPL are less effective on light, grey or white hair, a point electrolysis proponents emphasise [2].

Wikipedia states that laser hair removal has been FDA-approved since 1997 and sometimes becomes permanent after several sessions, whereas it identifies electrology as the method recognised for permanent removal [3]. A 2000 study of 12 patients cited in Wikipedia's laser article found laser to be about 60 times faster than galvanic electrolysis, though its authors noted that not all modern electrolysis methods were tested [5].

Commonly reported effects are redness, swelling and pinpoint scabbing lasting about one to three days, with stinging or pricking during treatment. Rare effects include infection, usually linked to poor sterilization, and scarring, mainly in people with keloid-prone skin or from improper technique. Grokipedia lists active infection, keloid history, recent isotretinoin use, pregnancy and pacemakers as contraindications in some practice guidance [2].

Grokipedia reports that the FDA proposed in 1982 to classify needle-type epilators as Class II devices requiring 510(k) clearance, that about 31 US states and the District of Columbia license electrologists with training requirements ranging from roughly 300 to 1,100 hours, and that a voluntary Certified Professional Electrologist credential exists [2].

Electrolysis is discussed in appearance communities as a way to reshape the hairline or brows, clear stray facial hair in people whose hair is too light for laser, and treat beard-area hair. Cost and treatment length are common topics, with Grokipedia citing full facial treatment as roughly $1,000 to $10,000 or more over one to two years [2]. Insurance generally treats it as cosmetic, with exceptions for medical need such as hirsutism or gender-affirming care [2].

No studies found for electrolysis hair removal specifically in the sources reviewed. Registered trials under the name electrolysis concern percutaneous electrolysis therapy for tendon and muscle conditions, which is a different technique [4]. Comparative evidence for hair removal is discussed mainly for laser and light devices, including a 2006 Cochrane analysis cited by Wikipedia that reported about 50 percent reduction for up to six months with alexandrite and diode lasers [3].

card.summary: Needle-and-current destruction of individual follicles, the slow, per-hair route to FDA-recognised permanent removal on any hair colour.
card.note: Courses can take 12 to 18 months or more; no hair-removal-specific trials were found in the reviewed sources.

quick.overview:
Electrolysis removes hair by inserting a thin probe into each follicle and using electrical current to destroy it. It works on any hair colour and skin tone, including the light or grey hair that laser handles poorly.

Because each hair is treated individually, small areas such as brows, hairlines or stray facial hairs can still take many sessions over a year or more.
quick.mechanism: Galvanic electrolysis produces a chemical reaction in the follicle, thermolysis heats it with high-frequency current, and blend methods combine both. The aim is to destroy the growth centre so the hair does not return.
quick.risks: Short-lived redness, swelling and scabbing are common. Infection and scarring are rare and linked to poor technique or sterilization, with higher scarring risk in keloid-prone skin. Practitioner licensing varies by US state.
